title: How Much Protein You Actually Need at Every Age, According to Experts
excerpt: From adolescence to retirement, protein requirements shift dramatically — and most Indian diets fall short across every life stage.
body:
• The standard 0.8 g/kg/day protein recommendation is a bare minimum — active adults and older people need 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg or more
  • Nearly 73 percent of Indian diets are protein-deficient, with women, adolescents, and elderly adults most at risk
  • Plant-based protein from dal alone requires 4 to 6 large daily servings to meet an active adult's needs — strategic meal planning with diverse sources is essential

Protein is having a moment. Supplement brands plaster it across gym billboards, wellness influencers build meal plans around it, and supermarket packaging increasingly leads with protein content claims. But behind the marketing noise, a straightforward question persists: how much protein does your body actually need — and does that number change as you age?

The answer, backed by mounting clinical evidence, is yes — significantly. And for Indians in particular, the gap between what the body requires and what most people eat is wider than commonly assumed.

The Baseline: What the Numbers Say

The Recommended Dietary Allowance for protein sits at 0.8 grams per kilogram of body weight per day. The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) pegs its recommendation close to this global standard, around 0.8 to 1.0 g/kg/day. For a 60-kilogram adult, that translates to roughly 48 grams daily.

But nutrition researchers increasingly argue this figure represents a floor, not a target. "These recommendations are based on survival, not thriving," noted Express Healthcare in a review of India's protein guidelines. The RDA was designed to prevent deficiency in sedentary adults — not to optimise health, muscle function, or longevity.

Age-by-Age Breakdown

A comprehensive meta-analysis published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine, examining 49 studies and 1,800 participants, has helped refine the picture across life stages.

Adolescents (10-18 years): Roughly 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg/day. This is a period of rapid growth where protein builds bone density, supports immune function, and fuels cognitive development. Yet many Indian adolescents, particularly girls, consume just 0.6 to 0.7 g/kg — well below what their growing bodies require. ICMR data suggests boys aged 16-18 need about 55 grams daily, girls about 46 grams.

Adults (19-40, sedentary): The RDA of 0.8 to 1.0 g/kg/day is adequate here. For a 70-kilogram man, that is about 54 grams. For a 55-kilogram woman, roughly 46 grams.

Active adults: 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg/day. Anyone exercising three to five days per week needs substantially more protein to support muscle repair, recovery, and body composition. For a 70-kilogram man hitting the gym regularly, this means 84 to 112 grams daily.

Pregnant women: 1.1 to 1.2 g/kg/day, or at least 71 grams total. Inadequate protein during the first trimester impairs placental development; shortfalls later affect fetal brain and organ growth.

Breastfeeding women: 1.3 g/kg/day — the highest physiological protein demand most women will face outside of elite athletic training.

Adults over 65: 1.2 to 1.6 g/kg/day. The European PROT-AGE Study Group recommends at least 1.0 to 1.2 g/kg/day for healthy older adults, with higher amounts for those managing chronic illness. Ageing triggers what scientists call "anabolic resistance" — the body becomes less efficient at converting dietary protein into muscle tissue.

"Older adults may need more protein to stimulate muscle protein synthesis and prevent breakdown. The quality of protein is also important, with animal protein being more beneficial than plant protein."

— Vedika Premani, Clinical Dietitian, Sir H.N. Reliance Foundation Hospital

India's Protein Gap

According to the Indian Market Research Bureau (IMRB), almost 73 percent of Indian diets are deficient in protein. Another study found that nine out of ten Indians are unaware of their actual daily protein needs, often mistaking carbohydrate-heavy foods for protein sources.

The consequences show up in population health data. One in three Indian children under five is malnourished, according to the National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2021). Nearly 60 percent of Indian women are anaemic, with inadequate protein intake during pregnancy a compounding factor. Among older Indians, sarcopenia — progressive muscle loss that begins around age 40 and accelerates after 60 — is rising sharply.

The problem is compounded by diet composition. Cooked toor dal provides approximately 7 to 8 grams of protein per 100 grams. For a 65-kilogram active woman requiring 78 to 104 grams of protein daily, meeting this through dal alone would require four to six large servings — an impractical volume that also brings significant calories.

Practical Strategies for Every Meal

Nutrition experts suggest distributing protein across all three meals rather than loading it into one. Research indicates the body can effectively utilise roughly 25 to 40 grams of protein per meal for muscle synthesis — amounts beyond this in a single sitting yield diminishing returns.

A sample day might look like: breakfast with curd (125 grams, about 6 grams protein) and two eggs (12 grams) for 18 grams total; lunch with two rotis, a katori of dal (8 grams), and a paneer dish (18 grams) for about 35 grams; dinner with sambar (8 grams), curd rice (6 grams), and fish or egg curry for 25 to 35 grams. That reaches 75 to 90 grams — workable for a moderately active adult.

Combining cereal and pulse proteins across the day provides a complete amino acid profile, even without animal sources. Leucine, the amino acid most critical for triggering muscle protein synthesis, is higher in dairy and eggs — something vegetarians can compensate for by consuming slightly higher total protein volumes.

What This Means for the Diaspora

For Indians abroad, many of the same dietary patterns — heavy reliance on rice and roti with modest dal portions — carry over. The difference is that diaspora communities often have easier access to diverse protein sources including Greek yoghurt, fortified plant milks, and quality supplements. The challenge is awareness: understanding that traditional Indian meals may need protein supplementation at breakfast and snack times, not just dinner.

Older NRIs face particular risk. Sarcopenia does not discriminate by geography, and the combination of reduced appetite and familiar low-protein meal patterns can accelerate muscle loss in retirement years.

What's Next

India's protein supplement market is growing at 8 to 10 percent annually, but experts caution that whole foods remain the better foundation. For the general population eating a varied diet with deliberate attention to protein at each meal, supplements are rarely necessary.

The more urgent shift is in awareness — recognising that the 0.8 g/kg minimum that has guided Indian dietary thinking for decades may need updating, especially as the population ages and lifestyle diseases climb. As nutrition policy moves from calorie adequacy toward protein quality, both India and its global diaspora stand to benefit from rethinking one of the most fundamental questions in daily nutrition.
